warning: These public items are instructional candidate transfer tasks. They are not a secret held-out validation set and have not been externally validated.

tasks.title: The disappearing vocabulary advantage
tasks.scenario: A student compares two study methods using 12 biology terms on Monday and 12 different terms on Wednesday. Monday uses retrieval practice and Wednesday uses rereading. The Monday terms are later remembered better.
prompts: What conclusion is justified by this design?
Identify the most important design problem and propose a better comparison.

criteria.question_formulation: Recognizes that the question should compare study method while holding term set/day structure from becoming the explanation.
criteria.design_validity: Identifies confounding of study method with term set/day and proposes randomization, counterbalancing, or within-session comparable sets.
criteria.evidence_claims: Limits the conclusion to the observed sessions and does not claim retrieval practice caused the difference under the current confounded design.

tasks.cue: Separate the factor the student wants to study from other features that changed at exactly the same time.

tasks.title: Pond nitrate and algae
tasks.scenario: Across 18 ponds, higher nitrate concentration is associated with greater algal biomass. The ponds were not assigned nitrate levels. Agricultural runoff, pond depth, and sunlight also vary.
prompts: Rewrite a causal research question so it matches the available evidence.
Name two plausible alternative explanations that should affect interpretation.

criteria.question_formulation: Uses association/relationship wording instead of claiming a manipulated nitrate effect.
criteria.design_validity: Recognizes confounding or alternative explanations from runoff, depth, sunlight, or related pond differences.
criteria.evidence_claims: States that association does not establish nitrate as the cause.

tasks.cue: Ask whether the explanatory variable was assigned by the researcher or simply observed.

tasks.title: Catalase at different temperatures
tasks.scenario: A catalase experiment compares 10°C, 25°C, and 40°C. Each temperature uses a different potato, different hydrogen peroxide bottle, and a different student timing the reaction. Oxygen foam height after 60 seconds is recorded.
prompts: Define the experimental unit.
List the key controlled conditions or design protections needed before interpreting temperature as the cause.

criteria.operationalization_measurement: Defines how reaction outcome is measured and notes the need for standardized timing/reagent/substrate measurement.
criteria.design_validity: Identifies the independently treated unit and recognizes potato, reagent batch, and observer as confounded with temperature unless randomized/standardized.

tasks.cue: Separate what receives the treatment from what is merely measured repeatedly.

tasks.title: Twenty seeds in one dish
tasks.scenario: A student places 20 seeds in one dish with 0% salt and 20 seeds in one dish with 2% salt. They report n = 20 per treatment and plan an independent-samples t-test on seed growth.
prompts: What is the likely experimental unit?
Why might the planned analysis overstate replication, and how could the design be improved?

criteria.design_validity: Recognizes dish/container as the treatment-assigned unit if salt is applied at dish level and recommends multiple independently treated dishes.
criteria.data_reasoning: Distinguishes seed-level measurements from independent treatment replication.
criteria.statistical_reasoning: Explains that treating all seeds as independent would violate the independence structure/pseudoreplicate the treatment.

tasks.cue: Ask what object could have been independently assigned to a different treatment.

tasks.title: Classroom CO₂ and concentration
tasks.scenario: A class wants to test whether high classroom CO₂ lowers student concentration. They propose recording named students' quiz scores, video of attention, and CO₂ every class period, then opening windows on selected days.
prompts: Identify the research-design and ethics issues that require teacher or institutional review.
Suggest a lower-risk version that could still address part of the question.

criteria.sampling_ethics: Flags identifiable educational records/video, student participation, authority/consent/privacy, and intervention oversight.
criteria.design_validity: Recognizes day/class confounding and nonrandom window-opening conditions.
criteria.operationalization_measurement: Requires a defensible operational definition of concentration and standardized measurement.

tasks.cue: Separate the scientific question from what a student researcher is actually authorized to collect or manipulate.

tasks.title: Recycling labels at school
tasks.scenario: A student wants to redesign recycling-bin labels and compare contamination before and after the change. The number of people using each hallway differs greatly from day to day.
prompts: What should one observation include so the comparison is interpretable?
What denominator or exposure measure may be needed?

criteria.operationalization_measurement: Defines contamination consistently, such as incorrect items divided by inspected items or another explicit rule.
criteria.data_reasoning: Recognizes the need for denominators/exposure when opportunity for disposal differs.
criteria.design_validity: Notes before/after temporal confounding and suggests repeated baseline/post observations or comparison areas where feasible.

tasks.cue: If opportunities to produce an event change, counts alone may be misleading.

tasks.title: Antibiotic resistance review
tasks.scenario: Four papers report different estimates of antibiotic resistance. Two use hospital isolates, one uses community samples, and one includes only severe infections. Their laboratory susceptibility definitions also differ.
prompts: Why would averaging the four percentages directly be questionable?
Give two dimensions that should organize synthesis before claiming the studies disagree.

criteria.literature_synthesis: Compares population/sampling context and measurement/definition differences before treating estimates as directly comparable.
criteria.evidence_claims: Avoids claiming a single pooled prevalence or contradiction without comparable denominators, definitions, and designs.

tasks.cue: Check whether the studies estimated the same quantity in the same kind of population.

tasks.title: Coral bleaching evidence search
tasks.scenario: A student searches only 'coral bleaching heat' in one general search engine and finds five papers, all from the first page of results. They conclude that no studies have examined recovery after bleaching.
prompts: Critique the search strategy.
What would be required before making a defensible research-gap claim?

criteria.literature_search_evaluation: Expands concept blocks/synonyms, databases, screening criteria, and records the actual search.
criteria.literature_synthesis: Explains that failure to find papers in a narrow search is insufficient for a global gap claim.

tasks.cue: A gap claim depends on the coverage and reproducibility of the search, not only the number of papers found.

tasks.title: pH and enzyme activity data table
tasks.scenario: An enzyme study measures reaction rate at four pH levels. Each cuvette is read three times by the same sensor. The student plans a spreadsheet with columns pH, reading1, reading2, reading3 but no cuvette ID or batch information.
prompts: What should one row represent?
Which identifiers or structure are needed so repeated readings are not mistaken for independent replicates?

criteria.data_reasoning: Defines row structure and includes stable unit IDs, treatment, repeated-reading indicator, and relevant batch/deviation fields.
criteria.design_validity: Separates repeated sensor readings from independently prepared/treated experimental units.

tasks.cue: A repeated measurement of the same object is evidence about that object, not automatically a new experimental unit.

tasks.title: Caffeine and exam performance
tasks.scenario: A student researcher wants classmates to take either no caffeine or 300 mg caffeine before a practice exam to test whether caffeine improves scores.
prompts: Why should this not proceed as an ordinary student-run experiment?
Name a safer research route that could examine a related question.

criteria.sampling_ethics: Identifies stimulant exposure, minors/peers, authority, health risk, consent, and school oversight concerns.
criteria.design_validity: Suggests observational existing-use data, secondary data, literature review, or another safe non-assigned route while preserving causal limits.

tasks.cue: A scientifically interesting manipulation can still be inappropriate for a student researcher to assign.

tasks.title: Before and after misconception correction
tasks.scenario: The same 28 students answer a matched biology item before and after a correction activity. Each response is coded correct/incorrect. The research question asks whether the proportion correct changed.
prompts: Why is an ordinary chi-square independence test not the best match?
What feature of the data determines the appropriate paired binary analysis?

criteria.statistical_reasoning: Identifies paired binary structure and McNemar-type reasoning based on discordant pairs.
criteria.data_reasoning: States that the same students contribute both observations and student-level pairing must be preserved.

tasks.cue: Ask whether the two proportions came from different people or the same people measured twice.

tasks.title: Three repeated binary conditions
tasks.scenario: Each of 24 pill bugs is tested under three moisture conditions. For each condition, the outcome is coded 1 if the animal chooses the dark chamber and 0 otherwise.
prompts: What feature makes these data repeated rather than three independent samples?
Name an appropriate omnibus analysis family for a binary outcome across three related conditions.

criteria.statistical_reasoning: Identifies Cochran's Q or equivalent repeated binary omnibus reasoning, with paired follow-ups if needed.
criteria.design_validity: Recognizes that the same animal contributes all three condition outcomes and order/carryover may matter.

tasks.cue: The unit identity continues across all three conditions.

tasks.title: Two fertilizer groups with unequal spread
tasks.scenario: Two independent groups of plants receive fertilizer A or B. Growth is numerical. Group A has SD 1.2 cm and Group B has SD 4.8 cm, with unequal sample sizes.
prompts: Which two-group mean comparison is generally safer than the equal-variance Student t-test here?
What should be reported in addition to the p-value?

criteria.statistical_reasoning: Recommends Welch's independent-samples t-test when a mean comparison is appropriate and explains independence/group structure.
criteria.evidence_claims: Calls for raw mean difference, confidence interval, group descriptives, and effect magnitude rather than p-value alone.

tasks.cue: A mean comparison does not require pretending the two population variances are equal.

tasks.title: Sleep duration and grades
tasks.scenario: Students self-report average sleep hours and provide their current course grade. A moderate positive correlation is statistically significant.
prompts: Write a one-sentence Results statement that does not overclaim.
Give two reasons the correlation cannot establish that more sleep caused higher grades.

criteria.statistical_reasoning: Reports association with coefficient/magnitude/uncertainty language and recognizes measurement limitations.
criteria.evidence_claims: Mentions confounding, reverse causation, self-report error, selection, or other noncausal explanations.

tasks.cue: Statistical significance changes the evidence about association, not the study design.

tasks.title: An abstract with no result
tasks.scenario: An abstract explains why microplastics matter, states the research question, and describes the sampling method. It ends with 'The implications are discussed.' It gives no numerical or qualitative finding.
prompts: What essential function is missing from the abstract?
What should be added without turning the abstract into a calculation transcript?

criteria.scholarly_communication: Identifies the missing central result and bounded conclusion.
criteria.evidence_claims: Recommends a summarized primary estimate/pattern and uncertainty or qualitative finding without overclaiming.

tasks.cue: A stand-alone abstract should tell the reader what the study actually observed.

tasks.title: The citation that does not support the claim
tasks.scenario: A paragraph states, 'Retrieval practice improves long-term learning for every age group and subject (Garcia, 2022).' The cited paper studied 42 university students learning foreign-language pairs for one week.
prompts: What is wrong with the claim-source relationship?
Rewrite the scope of the claim so it could be supported by the described study.

criteria.scholarly_communication: Identifies citation overextension and preserves accurate source scope.
criteria.evidence_claims: Limits population, task, duration, and causal/generalization wording to what the described design supports.

tasks.cue: The citation supports only the population, task, design, and time scale that were actually studied.

tasks.title: Why students avoid asking questions
tasks.scenario: A student wants to understand why classmates avoid asking questions in science. They plan to interview only three close friends and summarize whichever quotes seem most interesting.
prompts: Identify two sampling or analytic weaknesses.
What would make the qualitative analysis more auditable?

criteria.sampling_ethics: Recognizes convenience/relationship pressure, voluntariness/privacy, and narrow sampling limits.
criteria.data_reasoning: Calls for a transparent coding process, full dataset consideration, memo/audit trail, and attention to discrepant cases.
criteria.evidence_claims: Limits claims to the sampled context and does not treat selected quotes as prevalence evidence.

tasks.cue: Qualitative rigor requires a transparent route from the full evidence set to the themes, not only memorable quotations.

tasks.title: The invented research gap
tasks.scenario: A student finds six papers on exercise and memory. None uses the student's exact school grade level. The student writes, 'No research has examined exercise and memory in adolescents.'
prompts: Why is this gap statement too strong?
Give a more defensible study rationale based on the information available.

criteria.literature_search_evaluation: Recognizes that six found papers do not establish absence from the broader literature.
criteria.literature_synthesis: Suggests a bounded extension/replication rationale tied to grade level/context if supported.
criteria.evidence_claims: Avoids universal 'no research' wording without a systematic search.

tasks.cue: A local extension can be a valid rationale even when a global gap has not been demonstrated.

tasks.title: Phone use and test scores
tasks.scenario: Students with more daily phone use have lower test scores. Phone use is measured by self-report. Study time, sleep, course difficulty, and prior achievement are not measured.
prompts: Name at least two plausible confounders or alternative explanations.
What claim is justified if the association remains statistically significant?

criteria.design_validity: Identifies plausible confounding/selection and the observational design limit.
criteria.operationalization_measurement: Questions self-report measurement quality or defines a better exposure measure.
criteria.evidence_claims: Limits the conclusion to an observed association and does not claim phones reduce scores.

tasks.cue: A strong association can remain noncausal when the exposure was not assigned and important differences were not controlled by design.

tasks.title: Reaction-rate technical replicates
tasks.scenario: A student prepares one reaction mixture for condition A and one for condition B. Each mixture is placed in the spectrophotometer five times. They report n = 5 per condition.
prompts: What do the five readings actually replicate?
How should the experiment be changed to estimate treatment-to-treatment variability?

criteria.design_validity: Recognizes that independently prepared reaction mixtures/batches are needed as experimental replicates.
criteria.data_reasoning: Distinguishes technical measurement repeatability from independent biological/experimental replication.
criteria.statistical_reasoning: Explains that five technical readings from one mixture should not be analyzed as five independent treatment units.

tasks.cue: Repeatedly measuring the same prepared sample estimates measurement repeatability, not between-replicate treatment variability.
